<!-- Typesetting specimen. Placeholder text, not a proposed provision. -->

(a) **General rule.** Except as provided in subsection (c), a peacemaking communication is confidential and may not be disclosed by a participant, the peacemaker, or any observer, and is not subject to discovery or admissible in evidence in any proceeding before the {{court.name}} or an agency of {{nation.name}}.[^scope]

(b) **Privilege.** A participant may refuse to disclose, and may prevent any other person from disclosing, a peacemaking communication. The peacemaker may refuse to disclose a peacemaking communication of the peacemaker.[^privilege]

(c) **Exceptions.** There is no confidentiality or privilege under this section for a peacemaking communication that is:

(1) in an agreement signed by all parties to the session;

(2) a threat or statement of a plan to inflict bodily injury, including a statement that:

(A) names the person threatened; or

(B) describes when or where the injury would occur; or

(3) sought or offered to prove or disprove abuse or neglect of a child or of a vulnerable adult.[^exceptions]

```alternative A
(d) **Waiver.** The confidentiality and privilege established by this section may be waived only in a record signed by every participant and by the peacemaker.
```

```alternative B
(d) **Waiver.** The confidentiality and privilege established by this section may be waived in a record signed by every participant. The peacemaker's consent is not required, but the peacemaker may not be compelled to testify about a peacemaking communication.[^alternatives]
```

[^scope]: Specimen note. The phrase "proceeding before a court or agency" is meant to reach every adjudicative or investigative body created under the enacting nation's law. A long note tests how notes continue across pages: an enacting body that wishes to extend protection to proceedings in other jurisdictions would consider a separate comity provision, because a rule of evidence adopted by one government does not by itself bind the tribunals of another. The rest of this note is filler of the same kind, repeated so that the note is long enough to need more than one page at the smallest trim sizes. An enacting body would also consider how the rule applies to records kept by the peacemaker, to notes taken by observers, and to recordings made with or without the consent of the participants.

[^privilege]: Specimen note. The privilege belongs to each participant individually.

[^exceptions]: Specimen note. See also § 2-105. The exceptions in subsection (c) are exclusive.

[^alternatives]: Specimen note. Alternatives let an enacting body choose between policy positions without redrafting the surrounding text.
